title: Fabrizio Giugiaro’s Copper-Bodied Maserati Nods to His Father’s Legacy (and Baffles Me a Little)

body_markdown:
Not quite a year after[Giorgetto Giugiaro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/know-your-designers-giorgetto-giugiaro/) ‘s son, Fabrizio, designed an aluminum-bodied supercar for Mexican collector Carlos Peralta, he has penned a second one-off for the same client. The body for this second project, the Peralta D, was hammered by hand from copper.


The Peralta name references that this is a one-off commission for the multi-billionaire businessman, investor, philanthropist, and baseball club owner of the same name. Per the press release, “The ‘D’ was chosen to emphasize the bond between Carlos and his daughters.” (Logically enough, the previous commission was the[Peralta S](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/fabrizio-giugiaro-pays-tribute-to-fathers-famous-boomerang/) , a nod to his sons.) D also stands for “ *donne* ,” which is Italian for “women,” whom Fabrizio Giugiaro and his firm, GFG Style, gave special consideration when designing the interior. More on that shortly.


GFG Style


GFG Style


GFG Style


GFG Style


The copper bodywork, which looks nearly rose gold in these photos, is the most striking feature of the car, whose wedge-like silhouette harkens to ’70s sports cars such as the Lotus Esprit,[BMW M1,](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/history-of-the-bmw-m1/) and even the later DeLorean DMC-12—all penned by the elder Giugiaro. Unfortunately, this design isn’t quite as effortless-seeming as those cars. The cowl is a touch awkward, failing to balance the proportions of the passenger cabin with the rest of the body, resulting in a “top-heavy” look.


GFG Style


We suspect that the underpinnings are the cause: The Peralta D is based on the Maserati Gran Turismo, a front-engined 2+2 grand tourer; its predecessor, the Peralta S,[is an MC20 underneath](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/gfg-style-giugiaro-peralta-s-monterey-car-week/) , and the architecture of that mid-engine supercar facilitated a far more cohesive design, with a cowl that flows perfectly into the expansive glass cabin.


GFG Style


That said, the use of Maserati underpinnings makes perfect sense, given the elder Giugiaro’s decades-long relationship with the marque: He penned the 5000 GT and 1966 Ghibli, the aforementioned Boomerang concept, the third-generation Quattroporte, and the early 2000s Spyder and Coupé.


GFG Style


The goal with the Peralta D was “to create a true 2+2 Gran Turismo coupe,” and it borrows a flashy feature from the Peralta S: The windshield, roof, and doors swing up and forward in one piece. The D had to be a little extra, however, and so it boasts gullwing windows *within* that giant forward-hinged canopy plus two “wings” hinged near the spine of the car that facilitate access to the rear seats—”often difficult in coupé designs,” as the GFG Style press release points out. The treatment draws inspiration from the[1967 De Tomaso Mangusta](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/detomaso/mangusta/1967/1967-detomaso-mangusta-302) , designed by Giorgetto.


Upholstered in leather with real copper thread, the interior emphasizes lateral symmetry. The passenger side of the dash features a cluster that mirrors the one behind the steering wheel, only the right-side screen is a monitor, ostensibly for applying makeup.


GFG Style


GFG Style


If I may briefly interject, this “makeup station” is very strange in practice, if not in theory. It is a truth universally accepted that you check your makeup in the car after you’ve checked it in the bathroom, because everything *will* look different in natural light. A screen interjects a layer of artificiality, which is especially annoying in a car, where you’re trying to get that last-minute, “real world” evaluation of your look. (I am currently in the market for a compact mirror to keep in my purse specifically because I will not touch up my lipstick in my front-facing iPhone camera.) I give only partial credit for the mirror below it, because at that level, it’s not useful for evaluating anything above your collarbones.


If Peralta’s daughters directly endorsed this treatment, I would love to hear their reasoning—in that case, they clearly know something I don’t, and I would like to be clued in. For now, people, please do not reinvent the mirror—specifically, the one on the back of the sun visor, which is already at a convenient height, and adjustable to boot.


GFG Style


Despite the many nods to a discerning female audience, and the on-board champagne refrigerator and copper glasses, your author’s humble preference between the two Peralta commissions is for the S over the D. I don’t even mind if someone else must refrigerate my champagne, and serve it to me in a vessel made of a more pedestrian material than copper (glass has the distinct advantage of being odorless, after all), or if I must check my makeup in the sunvisor’s mirror.


GFG Style
